description_full: Millicom International Cellular S.A. engages in the provision cable and mobile services in Latin America. The company offers mobile services, including mobile data and voice, and short message services; and mobile financial services, such as payments, money transfers, international remittances, savings, real-time loans, and micro-insurance. In addition, the company provides fixed services, including broadband, fixed voice, and pay-TV; and fixed-voice and data telecommunications services, managed services, cloud and security solutions, and value-added services; and tower infrastructure and services. The company serves small, medium, and large businesses, as well as residential consumers and governmental entities. It markets its products and services under the Tigo and Tigo Business brands. The company was founded in 1990 and is headquartered in Luxembourg, Luxembourg.

financial_summary: Millicom International Cellular is a large-cap communication services business with a $14.0B market cap on $5.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 72% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.27× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 8.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 46% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 28% operating margin runs 19pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.37x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+12.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 169 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 99% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 24% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 0.73, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.17 vs 5y 0.59), so read it loosely.
About $75.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash and 64% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 56% below its DCF fair value of $190, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 86%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $131 to $287 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 24.7 vs 14.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 42% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $96.39 on average, 16% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.54).
It runs a 72% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.27x.
ROE of 37% is amplified by 4.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($1.6B of cash against $6.7B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.27 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.1% over 3 years and 6.9% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 40.4% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 12.3% on average.
Analysts expect 55.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 46.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 49%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $8.3M sold).
It returns 8.4% a year to shareholders (0.9% in buybacks and 3.6% in dividends).
The share count has grown 10.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 14,250 employees, each generates about $408K of revenue, 0.7x the Communication Services median, and productivity has risen 5.2% a year.
That works out to $76K of free cash flow per employee.
